Senses.Explanation: Juzhi’s One Finger names Juzhi’s recurrent public gesture and the case involving Tianlong, Juzhi, and the attendant boy. The Lamp Record supplies the narrative behind the label: Tianlong showed Juzhi one raised finger; thereafter Juzhi raised one finger to visiting monks; when a boy copied him, Juzhi cut off the boy's finger, called him back, and raised his own finger. Later records place ‘Juzhi's one finger’ beside Xuefeng's rolling ball, Yunmen's looking-and-‘look!,’ Muzhou's ‘ready-made,’ Deshan's staff, and Linji's shout as a named response associated with Yuanwu Keqin. Verses call it ‘one-finger Chan,’ say it was used throughout Juzhi's life, and repeatedly ask or comment on where he was accurate. The entry reports the gesture, its narrative, and its later case-label use; the texts do not supply a further gloss for what the finger denotes.

Senses.Explanation: The pair is spoken as advice, posed as a public question—“how do you understand it?” (汝作麼生會)—and reused in later appraisal and comment. One record pairs two people, “one stands on the high-high mountaintop; one walks at the deep-deep bottom of the sea” (一人高高山頂立，一人深深海底行); another expands the parallel with “one sails a boat on the mountain; one races a horse before the cliff” (一個山上行船，一個巖前走馬). Yuanwu answers the quoted pair with “a staff strikes a stone man’s head” (棒打石人頭). The phrase’s Chan deviation is this stable, publicly tested two-line formula, not an ordinary report of underwater travel.

Senses.Explanation: An 英靈漢 is an exceptionally capable fellow: a heroic man in the battlefield verse and, in hall addresses, the person able to step out, shoulder the work, or face the demand. Feiyin Tongrong says that going out from the crowd requires such a fellow. Huqiu Shaolong says only such a person can take responsibility and continue the house tradition. Dahui Zonggao pairs the one who can startle the crowd with the lion cub able to match a sage.
